meta.blurb: Ines Varga is paid to call an old iron bridge unsafe. But the iron is sound, and beneath it she finds twelve plates of letters that make no words. The man who hired her wants the bridge gone.
meta.bible: Ines Varga: a bridge engineer, patient and honest, our point of view. Tobias Wren: the museum archivist, thin and eager, ink on his fingers, wears a grey cardigan. Councillor Marcus Holt: smooth, silver pen, wants the bridge closed so he can sell the riverside meadows. Dr Sylvia Ashe: the museum director, about fifty-five, green jacket, silver bracelets; she secretly owes Holt money and tells him everything. Dale Kane: Holt's fixer, huge man in a donkey jacket and very large boots. Alma Dunn: the honest mayor of Harrowby. Constable Nina Brook: the local police officer. Amos Pell: the old bell-ringer of Saint Aldric's. Josiah Calder: the engineer who built the bridge in 1868, loved puzzles, wore a magnificent moustache. Ada Calder: his only daughter. Harrowby: the small town. River Wend: the river. Harrowby Bridge: the green iron bridge with three arches. Crown Mill: a ruined mill half a mile upstream with a stone crown above its water wheel. Saint Aldric's: the chapel on the hill; its bell was cast in 1868 and reads Ring for Harrowby. Calder's Gift: the legend and the truth, the riverside meadows and the bridge given to the people of Harrowby for ever. The cipher: the first message on twelve iron plates under the bridge is shifted by the digits of 1868, one, eight, six, eight, repeating, and reads Where the river wears a crown, look down; the second message on a stone beneath the mill wheel uses the keyword Ada and reads The bell keeps the key; the small iron key is hidden in the oak frame above the bell, stamped with a tiny bridge and the Roman number twelve, and it opens plate twelve, whose slot was painted over. Dr Ashe gave herself away by knowing about the hotel break-in and the keyword Ada before she was told. Voice and tone: lively, clear and clever, a fair-play treasure hunt with no violence or gore; Holt resigns and Kane is arrested. Added for the full-length book: Bea Hollis: owner of the Kettle Café on Market Square, brisk and chatty. Mrs Pike: landlady of the Wend Hotel, whose floors slope toward the river. Walt Fenner: the old river-keeper, who has watched the Wend all his life. Ruth Hale: an expert from the county record office, who judges old handwriting and paper. The Kettle Café: on Market Square. The town hall clock runs five minutes slow. Ines drives a red car. Ines notices every rivet. The inspection chamber is under the central arch of the bridge, reached by an iron hatch. The twelve plates are numbered in the corner; plate twelve has a keyhole-shaped slot painted over. The first cipher shifts each letter forward by one, eight, six, eight, repeating, so WHERE becomes XPKZF. Calder's notebook says a clever man should count by the year. Holt's plan: close the bridge on Saturday, then sell the meadows to a builder from the city. The report is due on Friday. Ines keeps her notes on her phone and in a notebook. Ines's false story: she tells Dr Ashe that the key is in the old coal store under the museum; that night Kane breaks into the cellar and leaves a huge boot print, which proves Dr Ashe passed the story on. The tower of Saint Aldric's has sixty-one steps. Amos Pell lends a rusty vestry key as a decoy; the real key travels in Tobias's sandwich tin. Mayor Dunn wears a gold chain; the town hall clock runs five minutes slow. Ruth Hale confirms the deed, letter and seal are genuine; the wax seal shows a tiny bridge like the key. Ines's laptop is found in Kane's van. Tobias becomes acting director of the museum; Dr Ashe resigns and gives a full statement. On the Saturday the town holds a party on the meadows and the bridge stays open; Ines is offered a new job in another town.

beats.scene: A red car drives toward a curved iron bridge over a river at dawn
beats.summary: Ines Varga, a bridge engineer, arrives in Harrowby at dawn and sees the old iron bridge over the River Wend.

beats.scene: A busy café on a cobbled square, with a woman pouring coffee
beats.summary: In the Kettle Café, Bea Hollis tells Ines that the whole town is talking about the bridge.

beats.scene: A crooked hotel room with a quilt and a window full of arches
beats.summary: Mrs Pike gives Ines a room at the Wend Hotel with a view of the bridge, already paid for by Holt.

beats.scene: Councillor Holt sits behind a polished desk at the town hall, smiling coldly
beats.summary: Councillor Marcus Holt receives Ines in his office, turning a silver pen in his fingers.

beats.scene: Holt leans across a shining desk, one hand held out toward Ines
beats.summary: Holt explains that he needs a report by Friday and hopes it will say the bridge is unsafe.

beats.scene: Ines stands, shaking her head, while Holt taps his pen on the desk
beats.summary: Ines says she never writes a conclusion before the survey, and Holt hints at a generous reward.

beats.scene: An enormous man in a donkey jacket leans against a lamp post
beats.summary: Outside the town hall, Ines notices a huge man in big boots who watches her cross the square.

beats.scene: A tired clerk unrolls old bridge plans across a counter
beats.summary: In the council office Ines studies the original plans, signed by Josiah Calder and dated 1868.

beats.scene: Ines rests a hand on a small iron plate beside the bridge
beats.summary: That afternoon Ines reads the plate on the bridge, which names Josiah Calder as its builder.

beats.scene: Ines sits on a hotel bed with a notebook and a cup of tea
beats.summary: That evening Ines writes three questions about the bridge and underlines one word: honest.

beats.scene: Ines walks along the bridge deck tapping the ironwork with a small hammer
beats.summary: At first light Ines walks the bridge and taps the ironwork with her hammer; every rivet rings true.

beats.scene: Ines kneels with a steel gauge and a notebook beside a row of rivets
beats.summary: She measures the rivets one by one and finds none loose and no more than surface rust.

beats.scene: Ines studies a curved iron rib through a magnifying glass
beats.summary: Through a magnifying glass she examines the great arch ribs and finds no cracks at all.

beats.scene: Ines in waders stands in the shallows beside a stone pier
beats.summary: In waders she inspects the stone piers in the river and finds the foundations firm.

beats.scene: An old man in a woollen cap rows a boat among the reeds
beats.summary: Walt Fenner, the river-keeper, tells her the bridge has stood through every flood in living memory.

beats.scene: Wooden stakes stand in a green meadow beside a river
beats.summary: Walt mentions that surveyors have been hammering stakes into the riverside meadows for the town hall.

beats.scene: A small round hatch with shining bolts under a dark iron arch
beats.summary: Sure the iron is sound, Ines notices an inspection hatch whose bolts have been freshly oiled.

beats.scene: Ines turns a spanner on a bolt beneath the central arch
beats.summary: Ines unscrews the bolts easily and lifts the hatch away, and a breath of cold air rises.

beats.scene: Ines lowers herself on a rope into a dark shaft with a torch
beats.summary: With her torch and a rope at her belt Ines climbs down into a narrow chamber.

beats.scene: A torch beam shows twelve small iron plates on a damp stone wall
beats.summary: In the chamber hang twelve iron plates carved with letters; the twelfth has a painted-over slot.

beats.scene: Fingers trace carved letters and a Roman number on an iron plate
beats.summary: Ines feels the carved lines on the plates; each has a Roman number from one to twelve.

beats.scene: Eleven rusty plates in a row and a twelfth with a painted slot
beats.summary: The first eleven plates are fixed fast, but the twelfth has a slot painted over long ago.

beats.scene: Ines holds up a phone to capture a plate in torchlight
beats.summary: She photographs every plate in its own frame, sure that each letter will matter.

beats.scene: A torch beam shows the year 1868 cut deep into iron
beats.summary: At the end of the row Ines finds the year 1868 cut deep, bolder than any letter.

beats.scene: A large man in a donkey jacket stands on a riverbank at dusk
beats.summary: Ines climbs out at dusk and sees a large man watching the hatch from the far bank.

beats.scene: Ines at a hotel desk, laptop glowing with rows of letters
beats.summary: In her hotel room Ines enlarges the photographs, but the lines of letters make no words.

beats.scene: Mrs Pike carries a supper tray up a crooked staircase
beats.summary: Mrs Pike brings supper and tells Ines to ask Tobias Wren at the museum.

beats.scene: A thin man with round glasses stands among old papers in a museum
beats.summary: In the museum Ines meets Tobias Wren, the archivist, with ink on his fingers.

beats.scene: Tobias spreads a faded drawing of a man with a great moustache
beats.summary: Tobias shows her a drawing of Josiah Calder, the bridge's builder, and calls him mysterious.

beats.scene: Tobias sits down heavily on a stool, staring at a phone screen
beats.summary: Ines shows Tobias a photograph of one plate, and he goes pale and sits down.

beats.scene: Tobias leans forward over a table, eyes wide, listening to Ines
beats.summary: Tobias asks where she found the photograph, and Ines describes the hatch and the chamber.

beats.scene: Tobias reads from a cracked leather book beside a green lamp
beats.summary: Tobias reads from an old book that Josiah Calder loved puzzles and hid riddles everywhere.

beats.scene: An old page showing a bridge and the words Calder's Gift
beats.summary: The legend says Calder left a secret gift for Harrowby, called Calder's Gift for generations.

beats.scene: Green meadows beside a river, with a burned town hall in an old print
beats.summary: Some say the gift is the bridge, others the meadows; the old deeds burned in a fire.

beats.scene: Tobias whispers across the table, glancing at the door
beats.summary: Tobias says Holt is quietly planning to sell the riverside meadows to a builder.

beats.scene: Ines frowns at a map of the bridge and the meadows
beats.summary: Ines sees that closing and demolishing the bridge would make the meadows worth a fortune.

beats.scene: A woman in a green jacket carries a tea tray through a doorway
beats.summary: Dr Sylvia Ashe, the museum director, brings tea, her silver bracelets chiming.

beats.scene: Dr Ashe opens the door of a quiet workroom with an oak table
beats.summary: Dr Ashe offers them the upstairs workroom and says she would love to help.

beats.scene: Ines holds a buzzing phone while prints lie spread on a table
beats.summary: Holt telephones to remind Ines the report is due Friday and to hint at a reward.

beats.scene: Tobias clears a big oak table while Ines climbs the stairs
beats.summary: Ines says she will write only the truth, then joins Tobias in the workroom.

beats.scene: Twelve printed rows of letters pinned along a workroom wall
beats.summary: In the workroom Ines and Tobias print the photographs and pin the twelve rows of letters in order.

beats.scene: Tobias writes shifted alphabets on a sheet of paper
beats.summary: They try moving every letter by the same number of places, one to twenty-five, without success.

beats.scene: Ines sits among sheets of crossed-out words and a cold cup of tea
beats.summary: Reading backward and every second letter also fails, and the afternoon ends in frustration.

beats.scene: Tobias hurries down a staircase carrying a small black book in tissue
beats.summary: Tobias remembers that the museum owns Calder's private notebook and fetches it.

beats.scene: A finger rests on a handwritten line in a small black notebook
beats.summary: In the notebook Tobias finds the line: a clever man should count by the year.

beats.scene: Ines studies the number 1868 carved on a stone wall
beats.summary: Ines wonders which year Calder means and looks at the date 1868 carved in the chamber.

beats.scene: Ines holds a pencil over a row of letters, Tobias watching closely
beats.summary: She guesses that the digits of 1868 are the key, with one, eight, six, eight repeating.

beats.scene: Pencilled numbers one, eight, six, eight written above rows of letters
beats.summary: She writes the digits above the letters of the first plate and moves each letter back.

beats.scene: The letters XPKZF turn into the word WHERE on a sheet of paper
beats.summary: The first five letters, XPKZF, become the word WHERE, and Tobias shouts with joy.

beats.scene: Two heads bent over a finished line of decoded words in lamplight
beats.summary: They decode all twelve plates, and the message reads: Where the river wears a crown, look down.

beats.scene: Tobias reads a decoded line by lamplight, Ines listening
beats.summary: Tobias reads the decoded message again; neither of them knows what a river could wear on its head.

beats.scene: A map of Harrowby with a pencil tapping three marked places
beats.summary: On a map they find three possible crowns: the weir, the bridge and the old mill.

beats.scene: Walt Fenner mends a fishing net on a sunny riverbank
beats.summary: Walt tells Ines that the old mill upstream has a crown carved in stone.

beats.scene: Tobias holds up a brown print of a mill with a stone crown
beats.summary: Tobias finds an old photograph of Crown Mill with a stone crown above its great wheel.

beats.scene: Ines taps a stone crown on an old brown print
beats.summary: They decide the mill is where the next clue must lie.

beats.scene: Dr Ashe pushes a tea trolley into a room of busy people
beats.summary: Tobias tells Dr Ashe everything about the crown and the mill, and she wishes them luck.

beats.scene: A hardware shop counter with torches, coiled rope and new boots
beats.summary: Ines buys torches, rope and boots at the hardware store before the shops close.

beats.scene: Two figures walk beside a darkening river path at sunset
beats.summary: At sunset Ines and Tobias follow the river path upstream toward the mill.

beats.scene: A ruined mill with a stone crown above a silent water wheel
beats.summary: Half a mile upstream, Crown Mill rises out of the dusk, its stone crown above the wheel.

beats.scene: A new padlock on a rusty chain and huge boot prints in mud
beats.summary: At the gate they find a bright new padlock and very large, fresh boot prints.

beats.scene: A reedy riverbank with a low stone arch where a stream enters a hill
beats.summary: Unable to open the locked gate, Ines remembers the old stone channel and finds a low tunnel mouth.

beats.scene: Ines crawls through a low stone tunnel beside a rushing stream
beats.summary: They crawl into the old sluice tunnel with torches, water running around their knees.

beats.scene: Tobias in a dripping tunnel, eyes wide in torchlight
beats.summary: The tunnel is cold and full of echoes, and Tobias admits he dislikes narrow places.

beats.scene: A great wooden water wheel hangs above a moonlit stone pit
beats.summary: They climb out into the stone pit beneath the great water wheel, lit by moonlight.

beats.scene: A mossy stone block carved with letters beneath a stone crown
beats.summary: Under the stone crown they find a block carved with a second band of letters.

beats.scene: Ines scrapes moss from stone letters while Tobias holds a torch
beats.summary: Ines clears away the moss and photographs the second message from every angle.

beats.scene: A torch beam sweeps through a dark mill above a stone pit
beats.summary: A door bangs above them and a torch beam sweeps the mill as heavy boots tramp in.

beats.scene: Two people crouch in shallow water behind a thick wooden post
beats.summary: Ines and Tobias hide in the shallow water behind a post, hardly daring to breathe.

beats.scene: A dark figure walks around the rim of a stone pit with a torch
beats.summary: The unknown man searches the mill for a long time, then leaves and the mill falls silent.

beats.scene: Two wet figures run across a dark field toward distant town lights
beats.summary: They crawl out through the tunnel and run across the field; Ines wonders who the man was.

beats.scene: A hotel room with open drawers and clothes thrown over the carpet
beats.summary: Back at the Wend Hotel, Ines finds her door open, her drawers pulled out and her bag emptied.

beats.scene: Ines holds a phone in a wet pocket beside an empty desk
beats.summary: Her laptop is gone, but her phone with all the photographs is safe in her pocket.

beats.scene: Mrs Pike in a dressing gown raises her hands in dismay
beats.summary: Mrs Pike, back from choir practice, is horrified and says nobody passed the front desk.

beats.scene: A tall constable writes in a small notebook beside a hotel door
beats.summary: Constable Nina Brook takes a report, though Ines says nothing about the plates or the mill.

beats.scene: Constable Brook examines a hotel door lock with a small torch
beats.summary: Brook finds no scratches on the lock, so the thief must have had a key.

beats.scene: Ines holds a bedside telephone, still in her pyjamas, at breakfast time
beats.summary: Next morning Dr Ashe telephones, anxious, to ask whether they are safe after last night.

beats.scene: Tobias sits pale on a hotel bed, polishing his glasses
beats.summary: Tobias arrives, pale and worried, and says only a handful of people knew about the mill.

beats.scene: Ines writes a short list of names in a busy café
beats.summary: Over breakfast at the Kettle Café, Ines lists everyone who knew about the plates and the mill.

beats.scene: Holt stands at the bridge railing, hands in pockets, speaking to Ines
beats.summary: Holt waits at the bridge and threatens to cancel her contract unless she writes his report.

beats.scene: Holt hands Ines an envelope as the wind blows across the bridge
beats.summary: Holt dismisses Ines by letter and announces that he will close the bridge on Saturday.

beats.scene: Ines reads a letter at a bridge railing while wind tugs the paper
beats.summary: Ines reads the dismissal letter at the railing; her contract ends today.

beats.scene: Ines sits alone on a bench beside a flowing river
beats.summary: On a riverside bench she weighs going home against staying to finish what she began.

beats.scene: Walt Fenner pours tea from a battered flask beside a small boat
beats.summary: Walt Fenner brings her hot tea from his flask and says nothing, which is exactly right.

beats.scene: Ines types on her phone, sending files by email
beats.summary: Ines decides to stay at her own cost and sends all the photographs to Tobias and herself.

beats.scene: Mrs Pike stands in a hotel doorway wringing her hands
beats.summary: Mrs Pike keeps Ines's room at half price and says she never liked Holt's money.

beats.scene: A stout woman with a basket of apples talks to Ines in a square
beats.summary: In the market square Mayor Alma Dunn says she hates the plan but cannot overrule the council.

beats.scene: The mayor speaks low while market stalls crowd the cobbled square
beats.summary: The mayor says only proof that the meadows belong to the town can stop Holt now.

beats.scene: Two people hunch over prints of a mossy stone block
beats.summary: Ines and Tobias try the year key on the mill message, but it gives only nonsense.

beats.scene: Tobias reads a tiny margin note in a small black notebook
beats.summary: Tobias finds a note saying that a loving man locks his best secret with a name.

beats.scene: Tobias takes off his glasses while Ines reaches for her coat
beats.summary: Tobias remembers that Calder had one daughter, whose name no one recalls, and they set out to find it.

beats.scene: A clerk carries a huge old register toward a wooden desk
beats.summary: At the parish office a clerk brings them the great register of births, marriages and deaths.

beats.scene: Tobias runs a finger down faded brown columns of ink
beats.summary: Tobias turns the pages and, near 1859, finds the name Calder.

beats.scene: A faded page entry beside a small margin note
beats.summary: The register records the baptism of Ada, daughter of Josiah Calder, his only child.

beats.scene: Tobias whispers a three-letter name in a quiet office
beats.summary: Tobias guesses that ADA would make a perfect keyword for a man who loved puzzles and his daughter.

beats.scene: Ines writes the word ADA repeatedly under a band of letters
beats.summary: Back in the workroom Ines writes ADA again and again beneath the second message.

beats.scene: Ines bends over a page as Tobias hovers at her elbow
beats.summary: The first word comes out clear as spring water: THE.

beats.scene: Tobias reads aloud while a pigeon flies from the windowsill
beats.summary: More words follow, and Tobias reads them aloud as they appear.

beats.scene: A finished line of decoded words under a lamp
beats.summary: The message is complete: The bell keeps the key.

beats.scene: Two people laugh and shake hands in a lamplit workroom
beats.summary: They laugh, shake hands solemnly, and then ask which bell the message means.

beats.scene: A small stone chapel with a bell tower on a hill
beats.summary: Tobias knows which bell: Saint Aldric's, cast in 1868, which reads Ring for Harrowby.

beats.scene: A chapel on a hill under a darkening evening sky
beats.summary: The chapel is locked at night, so they agree to visit Amos Pell at dawn.

beats.scene: Dr Ashe stands in a workroom doorway with a plate of biscuits
beats.summary: Dr Ashe comes in with biscuits and says: So Ada was the keyword, was she?

beats.scene: Ines and Tobias exchange a look across a lamplit table
beats.summary: Ines and Tobias realise that nobody has told Dr Ashe about Ada.

beats.scene: Dr Ashe smiles brightly, bracelets chiming, in a lamplit room
beats.summary: Dr Ashe changes the subject at once, and her bracelets chime faster than before.

beats.scene: Tobias nods unhappily beside a pile of papers
beats.summary: Ines tells Tobias she wants to test Dr Ashe, and he reluctantly agrees.

beats.scene: Ines whispers to Dr Ashe at the foot of a museum staircase
beats.summary: Ines tells Dr Ashe a false story: the key is hidden in the old coal store beneath the museum.

beats.scene: Dr Ashe grips Ines's arm, eyes wide, in a dark stairwell
beats.summary: Dr Ashe promises to tell nobody and squeezes Ines's arm with surprising force.

beats.scene: A hotel bedside telephone rings in the middle of the night
beats.summary: In the night Constable Brook calls to say that someone has broken into the museum cellar.

beats.scene: A broken cellar door hangs open, a huge boot print in the coal dust
beats.summary: At dawn they find the cellar door broken open and a huge boot print in the coal dust.

beats.scene: Ines whispers to Tobias in a museum yard as a bell begins to ring
beats.summary: Ines points out that only one person heard about the coal store, and Tobias whispers Dr Ashe's name.

beats.scene: Two people climb a grassy hill toward a stone chapel at dawn
beats.summary: At dawn Ines and Tobias climb the hill to Saint Aldric's chapel as its bell rings.

beats.scene: A bell-ringer in a woollen hat walks down a chapel path
beats.summary: Amos Pell, the bell-ringer, hears their story and agrees to take them up the tower.

beats.scene: A narrow spiral stone staircase lit by a torch
beats.summary: They climb the sixty-one steps of the spiral stair behind the wheezing Amos.

beats.scene: A great bronze bell in a thick black oak frame, open to the wind
beats.summary: At the top hangs a great bronze bell reading Ring for Harrowby, cast in 1868.

beats.scene: Amos stands by the old oak frame looking thoughtful
beats.summary: Amos says his family has kept the tower for four generations and always minded the old oak.

beats.scene: Ines runs her hand along a dark oak beam, Tobias holding a torch
beats.summary: Ines searches every beam of the oak frame, but each one seems perfectly ordinary.

beats.scene: A tiny wooden door opening in a high beam above a bell
beats.summary: Above the bell she finds a small hollow with a hidden door and presses its catch.

beats.scene: A hand drawing a cloth bundle out of a hole in a beam
beats.summary: She draws out a bundle wrapped in oilcloth and lays it in her palm.

beats.scene: A small iron key stamped with a tiny bridge and the number XII
beats.summary: Inside the cloth is a small iron key stamped with a tiny bridge and the Roman number XII.

beats.scene: Ines stares at the key while the bell hangs silent above her
beats.summary: Ines thinks of plate twelve under the bridge and understands that the answer was there all along.

beats.scene: Ines whispers to Tobias on a dim spiral stair
beats.summary: On the stair Ines whispers that they must hide the real key before anyone sees it.

beats.scene: Amos hands a long rusty key wrapped in oilcloth from a cupboard
beats.summary: Amos fetches a rusty vestry key from the chapel cupboard, and they wrap it in the oilcloth.

beats.scene: Tobias slides a small key under sandwiches in a lunch tin
beats.summary: Tobias hides the real key under his cheese sandwiches in his sandwich tin.

beats.scene: A chapel gate blocked by a woman in green and a huge man
beats.summary: At the chapel gate they find Dr Ashe and a very large man blocking the way.

beats.scene: A huge man in a donkey jacket folds his arms in a gateway
beats.summary: The man is Dale Kane, Holt's fixer, with boots as big as the print in the coal dust.

beats.scene: Dr Ashe holds out her hand, cold and unsmiling, at a gate
beats.summary: Dr Ashe coldly demands the key, and Tobias asks her why she has done this.

beats.scene: Ines places a cloth bundle in Dr Ashe's outstretched hand
beats.summary: Ines gives Dr Ashe the rusty key wrapped in oilcloth.

beats.scene: A car drives away down a lane under trees in a cloud of dust
beats.summary: Dr Ashe and Kane hurry away in a car with the rusty key.

beats.scene: Amos fans himself with his hat while Tobias opens a sandwich tin
beats.summary: Tobias opens the sandwich tin, the real key lies safe inside, and they laugh with relief.

beats.scene: Ines holds a phone to her ear on a chapel hill above a town
beats.summary: Ines telephones Mayor Dunn and Constable Brook and asks them to come to the bridge at noon.

beats.scene: A café table crowded with plates of eggs, toast and sausages
beats.summary: Ines and Tobias eat a huge breakfast at the Kettle Café while Bea Hollis listens to their story.

beats.scene: Bea Hollis takes off her apron and strides across a busy square
beats.summary: Bea declares that the whole town must come to the bridge at noon and goes door to door.

beats.scene: Ines hurries to a riverbank where an old man waits by a boat
beats.summary: Tobias stays at the café with the tin while Ines goes to Walt Fenner's boat.

beats.scene: A car stops at the end of an iron bridge; three people step out
beats.summary: From beneath the far arch Ines and Walt watch Holt, Dr Ashe and Kane arrive at the hatch.

beats.scene: A rowing boat floats silently beneath a central iron arch
beats.summary: Kane lifts the hatch, the three climb down, and Walt rows silently beneath the arch to listen.

beats.scene: Holt pushes a rusty key into a painted slot in a dark chamber
beats.summary: Holt pushes the rusty key into the slot of plate twelve, and a long scraping follows.

beats.scene: Kane scrapes at a painted slot with a knife in a dark chamber
beats.summary: The key will not turn, and Kane scrapes the old paint out of the slot with his knife.

beats.scene: Dr Ashe speaks nervously while Holt glares at her in torchlight
beats.summary: Dr Ashe says it is exactly the key Ines gave her, and Holt blames her angrily.

beats.scene: Kane swings a hammer at an iron plate in a dark chamber
beats.summary: Holt realises they were tricked, and Kane hammers the plate, but the old iron will not give.

beats.scene: A car drives away from a bridge in a spray of gravel
beats.summary: Holt orders them out, promising to return with a cutting torch, and they drive away.

beats.scene: A crowd of townspeople gathers at the foot of a green iron bridge
beats.summary: By half past eleven a crowd has gathered at the foot of the bridge, thanks to Bea Hollis.

beats.scene: Shopkeepers, children on shoulders and a bell-ringer in his best coat
beats.summary: Shopkeepers, children, Mrs Pike and Amos Pell join the crowd, with Tobias hugging the sandwich tin.

beats.scene: A mayor in a gold chain walks through a parting crowd beside a constable
beats.summary: Mayor Alma Dunn arrives with Constable Brook at her side, and the crowd begins to clap.

beats.scene: A car skids to a stop and an angry man jumps out
beats.summary: Holt arrives with Kane and a pale Dr Ashe and shouts that the bridge is dangerous.

beats.scene: The mayor stands calmly before an angry councillor on a bridge
beats.summary: The mayor replies that the bridge belongs to the town until Saturday, and the crowd laughs.

beats.scene: Constable Brook raises one finger before a huge man in boots
beats.summary: Brook politely tells Kane to stay where he is, and he stays.

beats.scene: Four people walk across a bridge deck toward an open iron hatch
beats.summary: Ines, Tobias, the mayor and the constable climb down through the hatch into the dark chamber.

beats.scene: A torch beam falls on twelve plates as Ines kneels at the last
beats.summary: Ines kneels at plate twelve and scrapes away the last flakes of paint from the slot.

beats.scene: Tobias hands a small greasy iron key to Ines in torchlight
beats.summary: Tobias hands her the real key from the sandwich tin, and she pushes it into the slot.

beats.scene: A hand turns a small iron key in an old iron plate
beats.summary: Ines turns the key, and with a soft, solid click the lock opens.

beats.scene: An old iron plate swings open to show a dry stone hollow
beats.summary: Plate twelve swings open on hidden hinges, showing a dry hollow in the stonework.

beats.scene: A torch finds a small green iron box with a bridge on it
beats.summary: Inside the hollow sits a small green iron box with a bridge cut into its lid.

beats.scene: Two pairs of hands carry a small iron box up a ladder
beats.summary: Tobias and Ines lift the box out and pass it up to the mayor.

beats.summary: Constable Brook studies her photograph of the boot print and looks at Kane's boots.

beats.summary: Ines reads a message from an engineering firm in another town offering her a new job.

A1A2: Ines drove into Harrowby early and saw the old iron bridge.
Bea at the Kettle Café said the whole town was talking about the bridge.
Mrs Pike gave Ines a hotel room with a view of the bridge.
Councillor Holt sat behind a big desk and smiled a cold smile.
Holt wanted the report by Friday and hoped it would say unsafe.
Ines said she wrote reports after looking, never before.
Outside, a huge man in a heavy jacket watched her walk away.
In the council office, Ines read the plans of the bridge from 1868.
That afternoon Ines stood at the bridge and read the name Josiah Calder.
That night, Ines wrote down her plan and promised to tell the truth.
Early the next morning, Ines walked along the bridge and tapped the iron.
She measured every bolt and wrote the numbers in her little book.
She looked closely at the big iron ribs and found no cracks.
Then she walked down to the river to look at the stone supports.
An old man named Walt said the bridge had stood through every flood.
Walt said strange men had put wooden sticks in the meadows.
Ines found the bridge strong, so she wondered why Holt wanted it closed.
Under the middle arch, she saw an iron hatch with shiny, oiled bolts.
She opened the hatch, took her torch and climbed down into the dark.
On the wall hung twelve small iron plates, and the last had a slot.
Ines ran her fingers over the plates, each with a line of strange letters.
Eleven plates were the same, but the twelfth had a painted slot.
She took a photograph of every plate with her phone.
At the end of the row, she saw the year 1868 cut deep.
When she climbed out, a big man was watching from the far bank.
That night, Ines looked at her photographs, but the letters made no words.
Mrs Pike said that Tobias at the museum knew everything about the bridge.
In the morning Ines met Tobias, a thin man with ink on his fingers.
Tobias showed her a drawing of Josiah Calder, who had a big moustache.
Ines showed him one photograph, and Tobias went pale and sat down.
Tobias asked where she found it, and Ines told him about the hatch.
Tobias opened a leather book and read to her by the lamp.
He read that Josiah Calder loved puzzles and left a gift for the town.
The gift was the meadows or the bridge, but nobody had ever found proof.
Tobias said Holt wanted to sell the meadows and build houses on them.
Ines understood that closing the bridge might help Holt sell the meadows.
Dr Ashe, the museum director, came in wearing a green jacket and smiling.
Dr Ashe said she wanted to help and gave them a quiet room.
Holt telephoned Ines and reminded her that her report was due on Friday.
Ines said she would write only the truth, and then she went to work.
Upstairs, Tobias and Ines put the twelve photographs on the wall.
They tried moving each letter by one place, then two, then three.
Nothing worked, and the letters still made no words.
Then Tobias remembered Calder's old notebook and ran to find it.
In it, Calder wrote that a clever man should count by the year.
Ines thought about the year on the wall, and her eyes opened wide.
She tried moving the letters by one, eight, six and eight, again and again.
She wrote the numbers over the letters and moved each letter back.
The first word appeared at last, and it was WHERE.
Together they read all twelve plates: “Where the river wears a crown, look down.”
Tobias read the message again, and neither of them understood it.
A crown on a river might be a weir, a bridge or a mill.
They asked Walt, and he said the old mill upstream had a stone crown.
Tobias found a photograph of Crown Mill, with a stone crown above its wheel.
They knew the answer now: the next clue was at the mill.
Dr Ashe came in, and they told her about the mill.
Ines bought strong boots and two torches at the hardware shop.
At sunset they walked along the river path toward the old mill.
Half a mile upstream, the ruined mill stood dark against the sky.
At the gate they found a new lock and fresh boot prints.
They could not open the gate, so they looked for another way in.
Ines and Tobias crawled through a low stone tunnel beside a rushing stream.
The tunnel was cold and wet, and Tobias hated every minute of it.
At the end, they stood in the pit under the great water wheel.
Under the stone crown, they found a block with a second band of letters.
Ines took photographs of the letters as fast as she could.
Suddenly a light shone through the mill, and heavy boots walked above them.
Ines and Tobias hid in the cold water and did not move.
The man looked around for a long time and then went away.
They crawled out and ran across the dark field toward the town lights.
Back at the hotel, Ines found her room open and her things everywhere.
Her laptop was gone, but her phone with the photographs was safe.
Mrs Pike had heard nothing, because she had been at choir practice.
Constable Nina Brook came and wrote everything in a small notebook.
Brook said it was a strange thief who took only a laptop.
The next morning, Dr Ashe called and asked if they were safe.
Tobias came to the hotel and said only a few people knew.
Ines made a list of everyone who knew about their secret.
At the bridge, Holt told Ines to write his report or lose her job.
Then Holt gave her a letter and said she was dismissed.
Ines read the letter slowly, and her face went cold.
She sat by the river and thought about going home.
Walt came and gave her hot tea from his flask.
Ines decided to stay, and she sent her photographs to Tobias.
Mrs Pike said Ines could keep the room for half the price.
In the market, Mayor Alma Dunn said she wanted to save the bridge.
But the mayor needed proof that the meadows belonged to the town.
Upstairs, the year key did not work on the second message.
Tobias read a note in the book about a name that opens a door.
Tobias thought of Calder's daughter and said they must find her name.
At the parish office, a kind clerk brought them a very big book.
Tobias turned the heavy pages until he found the name Calder.
Josiah Calder had only one child, a little girl called Ada.
Tobias whispered that Ada might be the key word, and Ines smiled.
Back upstairs, Ines wrote ADA again and again under the letters.
She moved each letter back, and the word THE appeared.
More words came, and Tobias read them aloud, one by one.
At last the message was clear: “The bell keeps the key.”
They laughed together, and then they asked each other which bell.
Tobias remembered the bell at Saint Aldric's chapel, cast in the year 1868.
The chapel was closed for the night, so they decided to wait.
Then Dr Ashe came to the door with a plate of biscuits.
She smiled and said, “So Ada was the keyword, was she?”
Ines and Tobias looked at each other, because nobody had told her.
Ines wanted to test her, so she made up a story.
She told Dr Ashe the key was hidden in the old museum coal store.
Dr Ashe smiled, said it sounded exciting and promised to tell nobody.
That night, someone broke into the museum cellar and left a large boot print.
At dawn the cellar door hung open, with a huge boot print inside.
Ines said only one person had heard about the coal store.
They climbed the hill to Saint Aldric's chapel as the morning bell rang.
Amos Pell, the bell-ringer, wore a warm hat and a kind smile.
Amos agreed to take them up the tower on a spiral stair.
At the top, a huge bell hung in a strong oak frame.
On the bell were the words Ring for Harrowby and the year 1868.
Amos said his family had rung the bell for a hundred years.
Ines ran her hand along the oak and felt a small hollow.
In the hollow, she found something wrapped in an old oily cloth.
The small iron key had a tiny bridge and the number XII on it.
Ines remembered plate twelve under the bridge, and she understood everything.
On the stairs, Ines whispered that they must hide the real key.
Amos fetched an old rusty key from the chapel cupboard.
Tobias put the real key in his sandwich tin under the bread.
At the gate, Dr Ashe and a huge man stood waiting for them.
The huge man was Dale Kane, and his boots were enormous.
Dr Ashe said, “Give us the key,” and her voice was cold.
Ines gave them the rusty key wrapped in the oily cloth.
Dr Ashe took it, and they drove away in a hurry.
Tobias opened his sandwich tin, and the real key was safe inside.
Ines called Mayor Dunn and Constable Brook and asked them to come at noon.
Ines and Tobias ate breakfast at the Kettle Café, and Bea listened.
Bea promised to tell the whole town to come to the bridge at noon.
Walt took Ines in his boat to the quiet side of the bridge.
Holt, Dr Ashe and Kane came to the bridge and opened the hatch.
Ines and Walt floated under the arch and listened to the voices.
Down in the chamber, Holt tried the rusty key in plate twelve.
The key would not turn, and Holt shouted at Kane.
Dr Ashe said it was the key from the chapel, and Holt was angry.
Kane hit the plate with a hammer, but it was far too strong.
At last they climbed out and drove away, very angry.
By half past eleven, a crowd had gathered at the foot of the bridge.
There were children, Mrs Pike, the baker and the two old bus drivers.
Mayor Alma Dunn arrived with Constable Brook walking at her side.
Holt came back with Kane and Dr Ashe, and he looked very angry.
Holt said the bridge was unsafe, but the mayor did not listen.
Constable Brook told Kane to stand back, and he stayed there.
Ines, Tobias, the mayor and the constable climbed down into the chamber.
Ines scraped away the last of the old paint from the slot.
She put the real key into the slot, and everyone held their breath.
She turned it, and the lock clicked open.
The plate swung open and showed a dry hollow in the stone.
Inside the hollow sat a small green iron box.
Tobias lifted the box out with shaking hands.
Inside were an old letter and a folded paper with a red seal.
They carried the box up to the bridge, and the crowd went quiet.
The mayor read the letter aloud, and everyone listened.
Calder wrote that clever and patient people could have his gift.
He gave the meadows and the bridge to the town for ever.
He wrote that his daughter Ada had walked on every plank.
The paper was a deed, and the crowd cheered loudly.
Holt shouted that the letter was false and that anyone could write one.
The mayor said an expert would check it, and nobody could leave.
Then Dr Ashe stepped forward and spoke to Tobias in a shaking voice.
She said she owed Holt a lot of money, and she was afraid.
So she had told Holt everything about the plates, the mill and Ada.
Ines said Dr Ashe knew about Ada and the hotel before anyone told her.
Holt said it was only Dr Ashe's word, and that proved nothing.
Constable Brook looked at Kane's boots and then at her photograph of the print.
The boots and the print were exactly the same size.
Brook arrested Kane, and Kane said Holt had given the orders.
Holt tried to walk away, but the mayor told him to stay.
In the afternoon, Ruth Hale came from the county record office.
She looked at the old paper and the ink with a big glass.
She compared the writing with Calder's plans and his little black notebook.
The red seal showed a tiny bridge, just like the key.
Ruth said that the deed and the letter were real.
The mayor said the council could never sell the meadows now.
Holt's phone rang, and the builder said the sale was finished.
That evening, the council met, and the hall was full of people.
Holt stood up, said he would leave the council and walked out.
Late that night, Constable Brook brought back Ines's stolen laptop.
Ines sat at the big table and began to write her report.
She wrote that the bolts were tight and the iron ribs had no cracks.
She wrote that the stone supports in the river were firm.
She suggested new paint and a few new bolts, and nothing more.
At the end, she wrote that the bridge was safe for another hundred years.
In the morning, she gave the report to Mayor Dunn.
At noon, the council voted to keep the bridge open for everyone.
Dr Ashe gave Constable Brook a full statement and left the museum.
Tobias said everyone could soon visit the twelve plates and Calder's box.
On Saturday, the town put tables and flags on the riverside meadows.
A brass band arrived, and a big crowd waited at the bridge.
The mayor cut a ribbon, and the bridge stayed open for ever.
Amos rang the old bell, and its song rolled across the valley.
Children ran over the planks, and Mrs Pike danced in the road.
At the party, Brook said Holt and Kane would go to court.
Tobias spoke about Josiah and Ada Calder, and everyone clapped.
Ines read a message that offered her a new job in another town.
At sunset, Ines and Tobias stood together at the bridge railing.
Tobias asked her to come back, and Ines said she would.
B1B2: Ines Varga drives into the town of Harrowby at dawn, with a long day of work ahead of her. Across the River Wend stands a graceful iron bridge, painted green and glowing in the morning mist.

The market square is only just waking up, and the smell of fresh bread drifts across the stones. At the Kettle Café, the owner, Bea Hollis, tells Ines that nobody in Harrowby talks about anything except the bridge.

Mrs Pike, who runs the Wend Hotel, gives Ines a small room on the second floor. From the window she can see the green arches of the bridge, and Mrs Pike mentions that Councillor Holt has already paid for the room.

The town hall is a tall building with a clock that is five minutes slow. Councillor Marcus Holt sits behind a polished desk, turning a silver pen in his fingers, and he smiles without any warmth at all.
Holt explains that the bridge is old, expensive and, in his opinion, dangerous. He needs her report by Friday, and he hopes, he says gently, that it will agree with him.
Ines replies that she has never written a conclusion before finishing a survey. Holt laughs, taps his pen on the desk and mentions that helpful engineers are always well rewarded.
As Ines leaves the town hall, she notices an enormous man leaning on a lamp post. He wears a donkey jacket and very large boots, and he watches her all the way across the square.
In the council office, a tired clerk finds the old plans of the bridge in a cardboard tube. They are signed by Josiah Calder and dated 1868, and the drawings are as neat as a piece of music.
That afternoon Ines walks to the bridge and reads the small iron plate at its entrance. It says only that the bridge was built by Josiah Calder in 1868, and she rests her hand on the cool metal.
In the evening, Ines sits in her hotel room with a notebook and a cup of tea. She writes three questions about the bridge, and at the bottom she underlines one word: honest.

Early the next morning, Ines walks the length of the bridge, tapping the ironwork with a small hammer. Each rivet answers with a clear, ringing note, and she smiles because a weak one would sound dull.
She measures the rivets one by one with a steel gauge and records every number in her notebook. Not one of them is loose, and the rust is only on the surface of the old paint.
Next she examines the great curved ribs of the arches with a magnifying glass. She expects to find hairline cracks, but the iron is as smooth and solid as the day it was cast.
At the riverbank, Ines pulls on waders and walks out to inspect the stone piers. Their foundations stand firm in the current, and the mortar between the blocks is still tight.

An old man in a rowing boat drifts toward her and introduces himself as Walt Fenner, the river-keeper. He tells her that the bridge has stood through every flood in living memory and has never so much as shivered.
Walt also mentions that surveyors have been pushing wooden stakes into the riverside meadows. Nobody knows exactly who they work for, he says, but they always take their orders from the town hall.

By midday Ines is quite certain that the iron is sound, and she wonders again why Holt wants the bridge closed. Under the central arch, a small iron hatch catches her eye, because its bolts are bright with fresh oil.
Someone has oiled these bolts recently, which seems odd for a hatch that nobody is supposed to use. Ines fits her spanner over the first bolt, turns it easily and soon lifts the hatch away.
A smell of rust and river water rises from the opening. Ines switches on her torch, checks the rope at her belt and lowers herself carefully into the dark.
At the bottom she finds a narrow stone chamber, and on its wall hang twelve small iron plates. Each one is carved with a line of letters, and the last has a dark slot hidden under thick paint.

Ines runs her fingers over the plates and feels the letters under her fingertips. Each plate has a small Roman number in its corner, from one to twelve, and a single line of capital letters beneath it.

The first eleven plates are bolted firmly to the wall, and their rust is thick and old. The twelfth is different, because the paint over its slot looks ancient, as if somebody wanted the keyhole to be forgotten.
Ines takes out her phone and photographs every plate in its own frame. She works slowly and carefully, because she has a feeling that every letter will matter.
Resting on an iron beam, she sees a date cut deep into the wall at the end of the row. It is the year 1868, the year the bridge was built.
By the time Ines climbs out into the evening light, her hands are black with rust. On the far bank a large man in a donkey jacket stands quite still, watching the hatch, and he does not wave.
That night in the hotel, Ines copies the photographs onto her laptop and enlarges them. She reads the lines of letters again and again, but they make no words in any language she knows.
Mrs Pike brings her supper on a tray and asks politely what she has been doing all day. When Ines mentions the bridge, the landlady says that the person to ask is Tobias Wren at the museum.
The museum stands beside the market square, and in the morning Ines goes inside. Tobias Wren, the archivist, is a thin, eager man with ink on his fingers and a grey cardigan buttoned wrongly.
Tobias is so pleased that anyone cares about the bridge that he forgets to be shy. He spreads out a faded drawing of its builder, Josiah Calder, a stern man with a magnificent moustache.
Ines hesitates for a moment, and then she shows him a photograph of one of the plates. Tobias stares at it, goes quite pale and sits down heavily on a stool.
When he has recovered, Tobias asks where she took the photograph. Ines tells him about the hatch under the bridge, and he listens with his mouth slightly open.

He reads aloud from a small leather book, and the old words sound like a story. Josiah Calder loved puzzles more than anything, and he hid riddles in his drawings, his letters and even his Christmas cards.
According to the legend, Calder left a secret gift for the people of Harrowby when he died. It has been called Calder's Gift for generations, but nobody can say exactly what it is.
Some people say it is the bridge itself, and others say it is the riverside meadows beside it. Tobias admits that the old papers were lost in a fire, so nobody can prove who truly owns the land.

Then Tobias lowers his voice and explains that Councillor Holt wants to sell the meadows to a builder from the city. The council owns them on paper, because nobody has ever found a document that says otherwise.
Ines sits very still as the pieces slowly fall into place. If the bridge is closed and pulled down, the meadows will be worth a fortune, and nobody will ever look under the arches.
A door opens, and in comes Dr Sylvia Ashe, the director of the museum, with a tray of tea. She is about fifty-five and wears a green jacket and silver bracelets that chime when she moves.
Dr Ashe listens with a warm smile and says she would love to help in any way she can. She offers them the quiet workroom upstairs, with its big table and good lamps.
While Ines is unpacking her photographs, her phone buzzes, and Holt's smooth voice fills her ear. He reminds her that the report is due on Friday, and he hints again at a handsome reward.
Ines says calmly that she will write only what she finds, and she hangs up before he can answer. Then she goes upstairs, where Tobias is already clearing the table for the twelve plates.

In the workroom, Ines and Tobias print the photographs and pin them in a long row along the wall. Tobias numbers each one with a pencil, and the twelve lines of letters look like a strange kind of music.

First they try the oldest trick they know, which is to move every letter forward by the same number of places. They test every number from one to twenty-five, but the first line stays as meaningless as before.

Next Ines reads the lines backward, swaps the vowels and tries reading every second letter. By the end of the afternoon, she has covered four pages with useless words, and her tea has gone completely cold.
Suddenly Tobias claps a hand to his forehead and says that the museum owns Calder's private notebook. He hurries downstairs and comes back, out of breath, with a small black book wrapped in tissue.
Its pages are full of tiny sketches and sums, and Tobias turns them with great care. At last he stops and reads aloud a short line: a clever man should count by the year.
Ines repeats the sentence slowly and asks what year Calder might mean. Then she looks at her photograph of the wall, where 1868 is carved at the end of the row, and she begins to smile.
Perhaps the digits of 1868 are a key, she says, with one, eight, six and eight repeating as the shifts. Tobias hands her a pencil without a word, and she bends over the first line.
Ines writes the numbers one, eight, six, eight, one, eight, six, eight above the first letters of plate one. Then she moves each letter back by its number, and her pencil moves faster and faster.
The first five letters, XPKZF, slide back by one, eight, six, eight and one places, and they spell WHERE. Ines stares at the page, then whispers the word aloud, and Tobias gives a shout of joy.
Working side by side, they decode all twelve plates before the lamps are lit in the market square. When the plates are joined together, they read, “Where the river wears a crown, look down.”
Tobias reads the message once more, and his voice drops to a whisper. It is a beautiful riddle, but neither of them can think what a river might wear on its head.
They spread a map of Harrowby across the table and tap three places with a pencil. A crown might be the foam at the weir, the arches of the bridge or something at the old mill.
At lunchtime Ines walks down to the river and finds Walt Fenner mending a net. When she asks him about a crown, he scratches his chin and says that the old mill upstream has one carved in stone.
Back at the museum, Tobias searches the photograph drawers until his fingers are grey with dust. At last he holds up a brown picture of Crown Mill, with a stone crown above its great water wheel.
They look at the picture for a long time, and Ines taps the crown with her finger. The message was written to be solved here, she says, and the mill is where the next clue must be.
Dr Ashe looks in with a tray of tea and asks how the puzzle is going. Tobias, too excited to be careful, tells her everything about the crown, and she says that it all sounds thrilling.
Before the shops close, Ines buys two torches, a coil of rope and a pair of strong boots at the hardware store. The shopkeeper asks where she is going, and she says only that it is a walk.
At sunset, Ines and Tobias leave the town and follow the river path upstream. The air is cool, the water is dark and quiet, and somewhere an owl begins to call.
After half a mile the mill rises out of the dusk, with empty windows and a roof full of holes. Above the great wheel, a stone crown still sits on the wall, like a hat on a sleeping giant.
Hope turns to worry at the iron gate, where a bright new padlock hangs on an old chain. In the mud beside it are fresh boot prints, very large and very deep.

At dawn, Ines and Tobias climb the hill to Saint Aldric's chapel, a small stone building with a square tower. The old bell is already ringing, and its deep voice rolls down over the roofs of Harrowby.

He turned a silver pen slowly between his fingers while he smiled, and the smile reached no further than his teeth.

Holt explained, in a voice as smooth as the desk, that the old bridge was costly, outdated and in his view a danger to the public. He required an independent report by Friday, and he trusted, he said, that an engineer of her reputation would see what was plainly there to be seen. The sentence hung in the air like a hand held out, waiting to be shaken.

Ines answered that she had never in her career written a conclusion before she had finished the survey, and she did not intend to begin in Harrowby. Holt only laughed, tapped his silver pen twice against the desk and observed that engineers who were sensible were generally rewarded very handsomely indeed. She wrote down three questions about the bridge, the report and the man who wanted it written, and she drew a firm line beneath them. At the bottom of the page, in capital letters, she added a single word that would guide the whole week: HONEST.
