She took out her phone and photographed each plate in its own frame, working slowly and checking every picture before she moved on. It was a habit of her profession that a drawing which omits one detail is worse than no drawing at all. Something deep inside her told her that every single letter was going to matter before the week was over.

When her legs began to ache, she sat on an iron beam and let the torch wander along the wall until it caught a date cut deep at the end of the row. It was the year 1868, the year in which the bridge itself had been raised, and the figures were bolder than any of the letters. Whoever had carved it had wanted it found, and had trusted that the right person would come along sooner or later.

By the time Ines climbed back into the evening light, her hands were black with rust and her jacket was stiff with river damp. She screwed the hatch back into place with care, and when she straightened, she saw a large man in a donkey jacket standing on the far bank. He did not wave, and he did not look away, and that was somehow worse than if he had done either.

That night in the hotel she copied the photographs onto her laptop, enlarged them until each letter was as tall as a thumb, and read the twelve lines again and again. They made no words in English, nor in any other language she could guess at, and the more she stared, the more they resembled a swarm of insects. She went to bed with the feeling of having been told a joke in a foreign tongue.

Mrs Pike brought her supper on a tray, asked politely what Ines had been doing all day and listened with sharp interest when she was told about the bridge. If it was old iron that troubled her, said the landlady, she should ask Tobias Wren at the museum, who knew every rivet and every rumour in Harrowby. She added, as she closed the door, that he was a dear, but that he talked.

The museum stood beside the market square, a narrow building with tall windows and a smell of beeswax and old paper that Ines liked at once. There she was introduced to Tobias Wren, the archivist, a thin, eager man with ink on his fingers and a grey cardigan buttoned wrongly. He blinked at her through his round glasses as though she were a rare book that had just walked in.

He was so delighted that anyone cared about the bridge that he forgot to be shy, and he spread out on the table a faded drawing of its builder, Josiah Calder. It showed a stern man with a high collar and a magnificent moustache, which curled at the ends like the scroll of a violin. Calder, said Tobias, had been the finest engineer that Harrowby ever produced, and quite the most mysterious.

Ines hesitated, for she was a careful woman and had known Tobias for less than an hour, but something in his enthusiasm persuaded her. She took out her phone and showed him a photograph of one of the twelve plates, with its tight line of meaningless letters. Tobias looked at it for a long moment, went pale to the roots of his hair and sat down heavily on a stool.

When he had recovered a little, Tobias asked in a whisper where she had found the photograph, and Ines described the hatch, the shaft and the damp chamber beneath the central arch. He listened with his mouth slightly open, like a child at a conjuror's show. Then he said that he had been waiting for most of his life for someone to tell him exactly that.

He fetched a small leather book with a cracked spine and read aloud from it beside the lamp, in the soft voice of a man reading to a child. Josiah Calder, the passage said, loved a puzzle better than a dinner, and he hid riddles in his drawings, his letters and even his Christmas cards. The old words made the whole room feel warmer, as though the lamp had been turned up a little.

According to the legend, Calder had left a secret gift for the people of Harrowby, to be found by the clever and the patient. Local people had called it Calder's Gift for generations, and they spoke of it half as a joke and half as a prayer. Nobody, however, could tell her what the gift actually was, or where a person might begin to look for it.

Some said the gift was the bridge itself, and others swore that it was the green meadows along the river, which the townsfolk had always treated as their own. Tobias admitted sadly that the old title deeds had burned in a fire at the town hall long ago. Without them, as Tobias pointed out, nobody could prove who truly owned the land, and so everybody could claim to.

Then Tobias lowered his voice and explained that Councillor Holt had been quietly arranging to sell the riverside meadows to a builder from the city. On paper the council owned them, he said, because nobody had ever produced a document that proved otherwise, and Holt had a talent for making silence look like consent. The price, he had heard from a friend at the town hall, was enough to make a modest man quite dizzy.

Ines sat very still while the pieces slid into place with the quiet click of a well-made joint. If the bridge were declared unsafe, closed and then demolished, the meadows would become a small fortune, and nobody would ever think to look beneath the arches. It was a very tidy plan, and she disliked tidy plans more than untidy ones.

The door opened, and in swept Dr Sylvia Ashe, the director of the museum, carrying a tray of tea and a plate of biscuits. She was a woman of about fifty-five in a green jacket, with silver bracelets that chimed softly whenever she moved. Her smile was broad and warm, and she seemed delighted to meet the engineer who was inspecting the bridge.

Dr Ashe listened to the story of the plates with every sign of fascination and declared that she would be thrilled to help in any way she could. She offered them the quiet workroom on the upper floor, with its great oak table and its good lamps, and she told them to take as long as they liked. Ines thanked her warmly and thought nothing of the offer at the time, which she would later regret a little.

While Ines was laying out her photographs, her phone buzzed, and Holt's smooth voice poured into her ear like warm oil. He reminded her that her report was due on Friday, and he hinted, with elaborate delicacy, that a very handsome reward awaited the engineer who wrote it. Ines felt the old distaste for flattery and bribery rise in her throat like something she had swallowed by mistake.

She replied evenly that she would write only what she found, and she ended the call before he could say another word. Then she climbed the stairs to the workroom, where Tobias was already clearing the table with the ceremony of a priest preparing an altar. Twelve plates were waiting, and they had been waiting for a hundred and fifty years.

In the workroom, Ines and Tobias printed the photographs, pinned them in a long row along the wall and stood back to look at them. Tobias numbered each one in pencil, and together the twelve strips of letters resembled the score of some very strange and very quiet piece of music. Somewhere inside that strange black pattern, Ines was quite certain, there was a tune that somebody had wanted to be played.

They began with the oldest trick they knew, which was to move every letter forward by the same number of places, and they tested every number from one to twenty-five. The first line obstinately refused to yield a single word, and by lunchtime Tobias had filled a whole page with gibberish. He ate a biscuit in gloomy silence and stared at the wall as if it might offer him a better idea.

Next Ines tried reading the lines backward, swapping the vowels and picking out every second letter, while the light moved slowly across the oak table. By the end of the afternoon she had covered four sheets with useless words, and her tea had gone as cold as the stone in the chamber. It was beginning to feel less like a puzzle than a personal insult from a man who had been dead for decades.

Suddenly Tobias clapped a hand to his forehead and declared that the museum owned Calder's private notebook, and that he had not thought of it in years. He hurried down the stairs two at a time and came back, breathless, carrying a small black book wrapped in tissue paper. He unwrapped it as tenderly as one unwraps a sleeping bird, and he laid it on the table with both hands.

The pages were crowded with tiny sketches, columns of figures and sudden jokes in the margins, and Tobias turned them over with a fingertip. At last he stopped, and in a voice that shook slightly he read out a short line written in a confident hand: a clever man should count by the year. Neither of them spoke for a long moment, because both of them could feel that something important had just been said.

Ines repeated the sentence slowly, tasting every word, and asked what year Calder could possibly mean. Then she glanced at her photograph of the chamber wall, where the date 1868 had been carved so boldly at the end of the row, and a smile began to spread across her face. It was the sort of smile that usually precedes a very good idea, and Tobias had begun to recognise it.

Perhaps the year was not a date at all, she said, but a key made of four digits, with one, eight, six and eight repeating as the shifts. Tobias handed her a pencil without a word, as one hands a scalpel to a surgeon. She bent over the first line of letters and began to work, with the pencil moving along the page like a small nervous animal.

She wrote the numbers one, eight, six, eight, one, eight, six, eight above the first letters of the opening plate, and then moved each letter back by its number. The pencil moved faster and faster, and Tobias leaned so close over her shoulder that she could hear him breathing. The whole room seemed to hold its breath along with him, and even the clock on the wall appeared to tick more quietly.

The first five letters, XPKZF, slid back by one, eight, six, eight and one places, and they settled into a single word. Ines stared at what she had written, then whispered it aloud, and Tobias let out a shout of joy that sent a startled pigeon flapping off the windowsill. It was a small word, but it was the first thing that Calder had said to anyone in a hundred and fifty years.

Working side by side, they decoded all twelve plates before the lamps came on in the market square, and the long scatter of letters turned into a sentence. Joined together at last, the plates read, “Where the river wears a crown, look down.” Tobias read it three times aloud, and each time it sounded more like an invitation.

Tobias read the message once more, and his voice sank to a whisper, as it does in a cathedral. It was a beautiful riddle, but neither of them could think what a river might wear upon its head. They looked at one another across the lamp, delighted and baffled in equal measure.

They spread a map of Harrowby across the oak table and tapped three places with a pencil, arguing cheerfully about each. A crown might be the white foam at the weir, the lifted arches of the bridge or something that belonged to the old mill upstream. Tobias favoured the weir, Ines favoured the mill, and neither of them favoured going to bed.

At lunchtime Ines walked down to the river and found Walt Fenner mending a net on the bank, his fingers moving with the patience of long habit. When she asked him whether the river wore a crown anywhere, he scratched his chin, squinted at the sky and said that the old mill upstream had one carved in stone. It had stood above the wheel for as long as anyone could remember, and the children of the town had always called it the Crown.

Back at the museum, Tobias searched the photograph drawers until his fingers were grey with dust and his hair stood up like a hedgehog. At last he held up a brown picture of Crown Mill, taken a century ago, with a stone crown carved above its great water wheel. It was a small, proud, slightly foolish crown, and Ines thought it the most beautiful object she had ever seen.

They studied the photograph for a long time, and Ines tapped the little crown with her finger as if to make sure that it was real. The message had been written to be solved in this town, she said, and the place it pointed to was the place where the next clue must lie. Tobias nodded so hard that his round glasses slipped down his nose and nearly fell off onto the photograph.

Dr Ashe looked in with a tray of tea and asked, in her warm and unhurried way, how the puzzle was progressing. Tobias, who was too excited to be careful, told her everything about the crown and the mill, and she said that it all sounded absolutely thrilling. Then she wished them luck and withdrew, her bracelets chiming faintly down the corridor.

Before the shops closed, Ines bought two strong torches, a coil of rope and a pair of sturdy boots at the hardware store in the High Street. The shopkeeper, a cheerful man with a pencil behind his ear, asked where she was going, and she answered only that it was a walk. It was nearly the truth, which she considered good enough for a shopkeeper who was already thinking about his lunch.

At sunset the two of them left the last houses behind and followed the river path upstream, with the water sliding beside them like dark glass. The air smelled of mud and mint, and a pair of swans moved away across the current with an air of offended dignity. Somewhere in the reeds on the far bank an owl began to call, and a second owl answered it from the trees.

After half a mile the mill rose out of the dusk, a tall ruin with empty windows and a roof full of holes. High above the great wheel, on the wall facing the river, a stone crown sat in the failing light like a hat left on a sleeping giant. Tobias stopped walking and simply stared, with the expression of a man who has just walked into the pages of a favourite book.

Their delight turned to unease at the iron gate, where a bright new padlock hung from an old and rusty chain. In the soft mud beside it were boot prints that were very fresh, very large and very deep. Ines crouched, held her palm above one of them and felt the hairs rise on the back of her neck.

The gate was locked and the wall was high, but Ines remembered from the old photograph that a stone channel had once carried water to the wheel. After ten minutes of searching among the reeds, she found a low arch in the bank where the stream ran into the hillside. It looked like the mouth of a very small and very damp dragon, and she hoped that the dragon was not at home.

They switched on their torches and crawled inside one behind the other, with water running icily around their knees and the roof pressing down on their shoulders. Ines pushed her rucksack ahead of her like a sled, and Tobias followed, muttering what sounded like a poem and was probably a prayer. The beams of their torches trembled on the dripping walls, and every drop of water that fell sounded as loud as a gong.

The tunnel was cold, wet and full of strange echoes, and Tobias confessed in a very small voice that he had never cared for narrow places. Ines assured him that it was only a hundred steps to the end, and she hoped fervently that she was right. Something small and soft brushed past her ear, and she decided not to enquire what it was.

At last the passage widened, and they scrambled out into a vast stone pit beneath the water wheel, which hung above them like the skeleton of a ship. Moonlight fell through holes in the roof in long silver bars, and the air smelled of moss and ancient oil. It was the most beautiful place either of them had ever been frightened in.

On the wall beneath the stone crown, half hidden by a curtain of moss, stood a great block carved with letters. They formed a second band of strange writing, similar in style to the one on the plates beneath the bridge, but plainly guarding a different secret. Ines laid her hand against it, and the stone felt like a sleeping animal.

She scraped the moss away with her glove and photographed the letters from every angle, while Tobias held the torch with both hands to keep it steady. Her fingers shook a little, partly from the cold and partly from sheer excitement. Each picture seemed to take a year to record, and every small sound from above made her heart jump.

A sudden noise made them both freeze, for high above them a door banged and a beam of torchlight swept through the dark mill. Heavy boots tramped across the floorboards, slow and deliberate, like those of a man who expects to be alone. Dust sifted down through the beams and drifted slowly into the light, so that each grain glittered like a tiny star.

Ines seized Tobias by the sleeve and dragged him behind a thick wooden post, and they slid together down into the shallow water at its foot. They stayed there, hardly daring to breathe, while the beam passed above their heads and moved slowly along the wall. The cold seeped through their clothes and into their bones, but neither of them dared to shiver or to make a sound.

The unknown man walked around the rim of the pit for what felt like an hour, swearing softly at the darkness, at the damp and at his own bad luck. At last his footsteps moved away, a door banged, and the mill went quiet except for the endless trickle of water. Neither of them moved until the last echo had died away completely, and then they waited another minute just in case.

They crawled out through the tunnel, soaked and shivering, and ran across a dark field toward the lights of the town, laughing in the high, shaky way of people who have just escaped something. Behind them the mill stood black against the stars with its crown still on. Ines kept asking herself the same question: who had the man been, and how had he known?

When Ines finally reached the Wend Hotel, she found her bedroom door standing ajar and the lamp still burning. Every drawer had been pulled out, her clothes lay in heaps across the carpet, and her bag had been emptied onto the bed like a fish onto a slab. She stood in the doorway with water dripping from her hair and felt strangely calm.

Her laptop had vanished, but her phone, with every photograph of the plates and the mill block, was safe in her wet pocket. Whoever had searched the room had been looking for something more precious than a computer. They had simply not been clever enough to look at the one object she never put down.

Mrs Pike came hurrying upstairs in her dressing gown and raised both hands to her face when she saw the mess. She had been at choir practice all evening, she said, and nobody she knew of had passed the front desk before she left. Her voice trembled with genuine distress, and she wrung her hands as though she wished to wring the whole night out of them.

Constable Nina Brook arrived within a quarter of an hour, tall and calm and smelling faintly of the night air, with a small notebook in her hand. She wrote down everything Ines told her, though Ines said nothing at all about the plates or the mill, for she had learned that evening to be careful. The constable's pencil moved across the page without any hurry, and her calm manner made the whole bedroom feel steadier.

Brook examined the lock and found no scratches, which meant that whoever had come in had either borrowed a key or been very good at pretending. It was a strange sort of burglar, she observed, who took a laptop and left a purse and a good camera behind. She promised that she would ask quietly around the town, and that she would let Ines know the moment she heard anything.

The next morning, before Ines had finished her first cup of coffee, the telephone on the bedside table rang, and the voice of Dr Ashe came anxiously down the line. She asked whether they were both safe after everything that had happened last night, and begged them to be careful, for the matter was surely more dangerous than it seemed. Ines was too tired to dwell on the words and merely said that they were fine.

Soon afterward Tobias arrived at the hotel, pale and out of breath, and he said that Dr Ashe had telephoned him too. He sat down on the edge of Ines's bed, took off his glasses and polished them hard, and pointed out that only a handful of people knew about the mill. It was not a comfortable thought, since each of those few people had smiled at them and wished them luck.

Over breakfast at the Kettle Café, Ines took out her notebook and wrote a list of everyone who had known about the plates and the mill. It was a short list, with a shopkeeper, a river-keeper, a landlady, an archivist and a museum director on it, and she disliked every name for the same reason. She could imagine none of them as a villain, and that was exactly what worried her.

Walking toward the bridge afterward, she found Councillor Holt waiting at the railing with his hands in his pockets and his silver pen glinting in the sun. In the same silky voice as before, he told her that her contract would be cancelled unless the report was on his desk by noon. His pleasant manner made the threat sound almost like a favour, which was exactly how he had meant it to sound.

Ines refused once more, politely and without hurrying, and Holt, sighing like a man disappointed in a child, drew an envelope from his coat and put it into her hand. It was a formal letter of dismissal, and he added, with a thin smile, that the bridge would be closed to everyone on Saturday. Then he turned on his heel and strolled away along the bridge, whistling a cheerful tune that made her blood boil.

Ines read the letter slowly, standing at the railing with the wind tugging at the paper as though it wished to take the news away. Her contract ended that very day, and the Wend Hotel, she realised, would no longer be paid for by the town. It was remarkable how quickly, and how completely, one could become a stranger in a town where one had begun to feel at home.

She sat down on a bench beside the river and tried to think clearly, which is difficult when one is angry. She could go home to the city and forget Harrowby, with its cold smiles and its cleverly hidden secrets, or she could stay and finish what she had begun. The river, which had heard such dilemmas before and had seen far larger ones, flowed on past her feet without offering any advice.

A boat bumped gently against the bank, and Walt Fenner climbed out with a battered flask under his arm. He poured her a cup of strong, sweet tea and said nothing at all, which was precisely the right thing to say. They watched the water together in a friendly silence for ten whole minutes, and neither of them thought that it was wasted.

In the end Ines decided to stay, even if she had to pay for every night out of her own pocket. She sent all the photographs to Tobias and to her own email address, because she had learned in the most practical way that a laptop can be stolen. It was a small act of defiance, but it felt a good deal larger than it was, and it made her smile.

At the Wend Hotel, Mrs Pike met her at the door, wringing her hands, and announced that the room was still hers for as long as she wished. She would charge only half the usual price, she added firmly, and she muttered that she had never liked Councillor Holt's money anyway. Ines was so touched by this unexpected kindness that she could hardly find the words to thank the old woman.

In the market square she met Mayor Alma Dunn, a stout and brisk woman with a basket of apples and an air of tired honesty. The mayor said that she hated the plan to close the bridge, but the council had voted, Holt had the numbers, and she could not overrule them. Her eyes said plainly what her position as mayor forbade her to say, and Ines understood them perfectly well.

She added in a low voice that the only thing that could stop Holt now was proof that the meadows belonged to the people of the town. Without a document, the sale would go ahead as soon as the bridge was gone, and the hands of the council would be washed clean. Ines promised that she would bring her something before Saturday, although she had not the faintest idea what that something would be.

In the museum workroom, Ines and Tobias printed the photographs of the block at the mill and tried the year key on them, one letter at a time. The shifts of one, eight, six and eight produced only nonsense, which meant that the second message was locked with a different secret. Tobias groaned, laid his head down on the table beside the cold tea and said that he wished he had been a gardener.

After a while he lifted it again and began to turn the pages of Calder's notebook, hunting for anything they had missed. He stopped at a tiny note in the margin, written in the smallest of hands, which said that a clever man counts by the year, but a loving man locks his best secret with a name. He read it twice aloud, and then a third time in silence, with his lips moving and his forehead creased with thought.

Tobias took off his glasses and said quietly that Calder had only one child, a daughter whose name nobody in the museum seemed to remember. If they could find it, he said, it might be the word that opened the second message. Ines was already reaching for her coat and her notebook, because she had learned to trust the beginning of a good idea.

At the parish office behind the church, a gentle clerk with a cough brought them the great register of births, marriages and deaths. The book was so heavy that Tobias needed both arms to carry it to the desk, and it smelled of damp wool and old candles. He opened it with the reverence of a man entering a chapel, and the pages gave a long, soft sigh.

He turned the thick pages carefully, running a finger down each column of faded brown ink, while Ines kept watch over his shoulder. Near the year 1859 he stopped, and his lips began to move as he read the name Calder. A moment later he gave a small, strangled cry that made the clerk at the far desk look up with alarm.

The entry recorded the baptism of a girl called Ada, the daughter of Josiah Calder, engineer, and a note in the margin showed that her mother had died soon afterward. It followed that Ada was Josiah's only child, the one person in the world for whom he would have built a puzzle out of love. Tobias read the line three times over, as if he feared that the ink might change its mind if he looked away.

He whispered the name aloud, and in the quiet office it sounded like a small bell. It had only three letters, he said, but it was exactly the sort of word that a clever father might choose to lock a secret that belonged to the town. Ines nodded slowly, feeling the idea settle into place like a stone in its socket.

Back in the workroom, she wrote the word ADA again and again beneath the letters of the second message, until the whole length of it was covered in a repeating pattern. Each letter of the key told her how far to move the letter above it, and the system was as neat as a sewing pattern. She started at the very beginning of the message and did not look up again until her neck began to ache.

She worked slowly at first, checking each step twice, while Tobias hovered at her elbow and hardly dared to breathe. Then the first word emerged, as clear as spring water, and it was THE. The relief was so great that she laughed out loud, and Tobias, who had been holding his breath, let it out in a whoosh.

More words followed, one after another, and Tobias read them aloud as they appeared, his voice rising with each. By the third word the pigeon on the windowsill had lost its nerve and flown away in a flurry of grey feathers. By the fourth, Ines was holding her pencil so tightly that it was in danger of snapping.

At last the message was complete, and she read it aloud in a trembling voice: “The bell keeps the key.” Nobody spoke for a long moment, because the answer had suddenly become very close. Even the clock on the wall seemed to be listening, and its slow ticking sounded like a heart beating in the quiet room.

They stared at each other, and then they laughed and shook hands very solemnly, like two ambassadors signing a treaty. After a moment Ines asked the only question that remained, which was also the hardest: which bell? Harrowby, as far as she could tell from a quick count on her fingers, had no shortage of them, and they were all different.

Tobias thought aloud about the school bell, the town clock and the dinner bell at the hotel, and then he clapped his hands together so loudly that Ines jumped. The bell at Saint Aldric's chapel on the hill had been cast in 1868, he said, in the very same year as the bridge. It bore a line of words that every child in Harrowby could recite: Ring for Harrowby.

The chapel on the hill was locked at night, Tobias explained, and Amos Pell, the old bell-ringer, never opened it before dawn. They agreed to wait, though it is hard to be patient when an answer is so close that one can almost hear it ringing. Ines folded her photographs carefully into her bag and tried to look calm, although her heart was racing like a drum.

As they were packing up for the evening, the workroom door opened, and Dr Ashe came in with a plate of biscuits and her bracelets chiming. She smiled her warm, bright smile and remarked, quite lightly, “So Ada was the keyword, was she?” It sounded like a friendly guess, but it did not feel like one, and the hairs on Ines's arm rose to prove it.

Ines and Tobias glanced at each other across the table, and in that look the whole of the afternoon seemed to change. They had not breathed a word about Ada to anybody, and the clerk at the parish office was the only other person who knew what they had found. The silence in the room grew thick and heavy, like honey going cold on a winter morning, and no one seemed willing to break it.

Dr Ashe changed the subject at once, asking about the biscuits and the weather and whether anyone had seen the evening paper. Her smile did not slip for an instant, but her bracelets chimed a little faster than before, like a clock that had been wound too tight. Then she wished them a pleasant goodnight, gathered her bracelets with one hand and left the room a little faster than she had arrived.

When she had gone, Ines whispered that she wanted to test something, and Tobias nodded unhappily, because he was beginning to guess what she meant. He had worked beside Dr Ashe for twelve years, and he did not want the guess to be true. Ines promised that it would be quick and kind, and that she would stop at once if she felt that it was cruel.

She caught up with Dr Ashe in the corridor by the stairs and told her, in a conspiratorial whisper, that the second message pointed to the old coal store beneath the museum. She asked her to keep it secret until the morning, adding with great seriousness that nobody else must hear a word. It was, of course, a story with no truth in it at all, invented in a moment by a woman who disliked inventing.

Dr Ashe's eyes widened, and then she smiled and said that it all sounded wonderfully exciting. She swore on her honour that she would not tell a living soul, and she squeezed Ines's arm with surprising force. Her bracelets were still chiming as she disappeared into the dark of the stairwell.

Ines slept badly that night in the Wend Hotel, listening to the church clock count the hours. Not long after midnight the telephone rang, and Constable Brook's level voice informed her that someone had broken into the museum cellar. She suggested that Ines come at first light, and Ines did not need to be asked twice.

At dawn Ines and Tobias stood in the museum yard, where the cellar door hung open on one hinge and the lock lay twisted in the grass. Inside, in a thin layer of black coal dust, was a single boot print so large that it might have been made by a small horse. Brook crouched beside it with a camera and a face like stone, and she photographed it from four different angles without saying a word.

Ines drew Tobias quietly aside and said that only one person in the world had heard about the coal store. Tobias went as white as paper, and for a long time he said nothing at all, and then he whispered Dr Ashe's name as though it hurt him. Somewhere on the hill above them a lone bell was beginning to ring, slow and deep, as though it were calling them to a decision.

They climbed the hill to Saint Aldric's chapel at dawn, a small stone building crowned by a square tower, while the great bell above it was already speaking across the valley. Its deep voice rolled down over the roofs of Harrowby and out across the water, and it sounded like a promise made a long time ago. Ines found that she was climbing faster than she had meant to, and that Tobias was puffing along gamely behind her.

The bell-ringer, Amos Pell, came down the path in a woollen hat and a coat that had been patched many times, wiping his hands on his sleeves. He listened to their story with his head on one side, like a thoughtful bird, and then agreed with a slow smile to take them up. Some of the best people, Ines reflected, are the ones who ask the fewest questions.

The stair inside the tower was narrow and spiral and smelled of dust and cold stone, and Amos climbed ahead of them, wheezing contentedly. There were exactly sixty-one steps, he announced over his shoulder, and he had counted them every morning for forty years. Tobias, following behind with a torch, reached the top in a state of heroic exhaustion.

At the top, in a chamber open to the wind on four sides, hung a great bronze bell in a thick frame of black oak. Around its rim, in raised letters worn smooth by weather, ran the words Ring for Harrowby, and beneath them the year 1868. Ines felt the date go through her like a note struck on the bell itself, and she held very still until the feeling had passed.

Amos explained that bell-ringers in his family had kept this tower for four generations and that nobody had ever found anything unusual in it. Still, he had always been told, by his father and by his father's father, to take good care of the old oak. He had never asked why, and now he looked at it with new and thoughtful eyes.

Ines walked slowly around the frame and ran her hand along each beam, while Tobias held the torch and tried to look as though he were not hoping. Every board was solid, dry and perfectly ordinary, and the minutes began to pile up like snow. She refused to be discouraged, since Calder had never been a man to make things easy.

At the highest beam, just above the curve of the bell, her fingers met a small hollow, no wider than a matchbox, with a neat little door in the wood. She stretched up on her toes, felt a tiny catch and pressed it gently with her thumbnail. The door swung open with a sigh that had waited a hundred and fifty years to be heard.

Her fingertips closed on something soft and heavy, wrapped in a greasy cloth, and for a moment she was afraid to move. Slowly she drew it out and laid it in the palm of her hand, where it sat as light and as significant as a sleeping bird. Amos took off his hat without seeming to know that he had done so.

Tobias shone the torch while she unwrapped the oilcloth, fold after careful fold, until the last layer fell away. Inside lay a small iron key, black with age but perfectly whole, and stamped upon its head were a tiny bridge and the Roman number XII. Nobody in the chamber said a word, and the wind sang quietly through the old oak.

Ines stared at the key and thought of the twelfth plate in the chamber beneath the bridge, with its slot painted over so long ago. The answer had been waiting under the bridge from the very start, she realised, hidden in the one place where nobody would think to look. Calder had sent them all the way around the town to teach them to look at what they already knew.

On the way down the spiral stair, Ines whispered that someone might be waiting for them at the bottom, and that the key must be hidden before anyone saw it. The big boot print in the museum cellar had left her with an uncomfortable feeling about the whole morning. Tobias and Amos listened gravely, and nobody made a joke, because they all felt that the morning had suddenly become serious.

Amos, who had been thinking quietly, suddenly said that he knew what to do and hurried to the cupboard in the vestry. He came back with a long, rusty key that opened nothing more important than the chapel's own vestry door, and together they wrapped it in the old oilcloth. It looked, in its greasy wrapping, exactly like the real treasure, and Ines privately thought it a rather splendid fraud.

Tobias lifted the lid of his sandwich tin and slid the real key underneath his cheese sandwiches, patting the bread flat with the care of a conjuror. Nobody in the history of Harrowby had ever stolen a sandwich tin, he observed, and Ines told him with total sincerity that he was a genius. He closed the lid with a satisfied click and tucked the tin under his arm like a man carrying a baby.

When they stepped out of the chapel into the pale morning light, they found that the gate was blocked. Dr Ashe stood in the middle of it, in her green jacket and silver bracelets, and beside her loomed a man so large that he seemed to have been built for a different kind of building. The morning air suddenly felt thinner, as though someone had opened a window high above them and let all the warmth escape.

The man was Dale Kane, Councillor Holt's fixer, and his boots were exactly as large as the print in the coal dust had promised. He folded his enormous arms and gave a slow smile, and the whole gateway disappeared behind his shoulders. Ines noticed that he was breathing slowly, like a man who has never been in a hurry.

Dr Ashe did not smile this time, and her voice had lost every trace of its warmth. She said that they had found the key, that it belonged to people who had a better use for it, and that she would be grateful if Ines would hand it over without any fuss. Her bracelets did not chime, because she held her hand perfectly still, and the stillness was somehow more frightening than any sound.

Tobias stared at her with his mouth open and asked, in a voice that cracked in the middle, why she had done this. Dr Ashe looked away, at the grass, at the sky, at anything else, and did not answer. Slowly, with her eyes steady, Ines put the oilcloth bundle into her outstretched hand.

Dr Ashe unfolded the cloth just far enough to see the dark iron and nodded sharply to Kane, who grunted like a satisfied bear. The pair of them hurried down the lane toward a car parked beneath the trees, and the sound of her bracelets faded and was lost in the noise of the engine. The car vanished around the bend in a cloud of dust, and the silence that it left behind felt strangely enormous.

Amos sat down on the low wall, shaking slightly and fanning himself with his hat, while Tobias opened the sandwich tin with trembling fingers. The real key lay safe on a bed of bread, as neat as a jewel in a box, and the three of them burst out laughing at once. It was the kind of laughter that has a great deal of fear in it.

Ines took out her phone and called Mayor Dunn and Constable Brook, one after the other, and explained in a few steady sentences exactly where the key had been found. She asked them both to come to the bridge at noon, and she promised that it would be worth every minute of their time. The mayor said yes at once, and the constable said that she would bring her best notebook.

In the Kettle Café, Ines and Tobias ordered an enormous breakfast, since neither had eaten properly for a day and a night. Bea Hollis set the plates down, listened with her head tilted to the story that spilled out between mouthfuls, and slowly sat down at the table. By the end she had completely forgotten the kettle, which was starting to scream in the corner like a small and angry bird.

When they had finished, Bea declared that the whole town should come to the bridge at noon, and that she knew exactly how to arrange it. She took off her apron, folded it neatly and marched out to knock on every door in the market square. Ines had never seen anyone look so much like an army, and she felt rather sorry for any man who stood in Bea's way.

Tobias stayed safely in the café with the sandwich tin on his knees, guarded by two retired bus drivers who had been persuaded to do the job. Ines hurried down to the river, where Walt Fenner was waiting by his boat with the air of a man who had expected her. He handed her an oar without a word, and she understood that this was the whole of the briefing.

From the quiet water beneath the far arch, Ines and Walt watched the bridge through the reeds. Soon a car drew up at the end of the deck, and Councillor Holt, Dr Ashe and Dale Kane climbed out and walked briskly to the hatch. Holt looked over his shoulder twice, like a man who has never been honest and therefore expects everyone else to be watching.

Kane lifted the hatch with one hand, and the three of them descended into the chamber one by one, the large man last and slowest. Walt rowed without a sound beneath the central arch, where the old iron shaft carried every voice upward as clearly as a speaking tube. They shipped the oars and let the boat drift slowly, and they listened with the stillness of two people holding their breath.

Holt's voice, impatient and sharp, echoed out of the hatch, demanding the key at once. Dr Ashe handed it over, and he pushed it into the painted slot of the twelfth plate with a grunt of triumph. A long scraping sound followed, then a silence, and then a very ugly word.

The key refused to turn, and Holt told Kane to scrape the old paint out of the slot with his knife. Kane obeyed, grunting and sniffing, but the more he scraped, the more obstinately the key stuck fast. Ines pressed her lips together to keep from laughing, and Walt, beside her, shook silently with a joy that rocked the boat.

Dr Ashe said in a small voice that it was precisely the key that Ines had given her, wrapped in the same cloth, and that she had seen no other. Holt turned on her angrily and demanded to know how she could be so gullible, while she stammered that nobody could possibly have guessed. It was the sound of a partnership beginning to crack, and Ines found that she was listening to it with considerable pleasure.

Slowly the truth dawned on Holt, and his voice rose to a bellow that rattled the shaft: they had been tricked, tricked by a bridge engineer and a man in a cardigan. Kane seized a hammer and struck the plate with all his strength, but the old iron only rang like a cathedral bell and did not give an inch. The echo went on for a long time afterward, rolling around the stone chamber like a great bronze note that refused to die.

At last Holt ordered the others out, announcing that he would return in the afternoon with a cutting torch and no more nonsense. They climbed out of the hatch one by one, banged the doors of their car and drove off in a spray of gravel, and Walt turned to Ines with a grin that stretched across his weathered face. The church clock was striking ten, and the whole town, as yet unaware of how much was about to happen, went about its business.

By half past eleven, a crowd had gathered at the foot of the bridge, and more people were arriving every minute. Bea Hollis had done her work superbly, and it seemed that the whole of Harrowby had put down its shopping and come to see. Ines, climbing out of Walt's boat on shaking legs, felt her knees go suddenly weak when she saw how many people had come.

There were shopkeepers in aprons, children perched on their fathers' shoulders and the man from the hardware store with a pencil still behind his ear. Mrs Pike had closed the hotel for an hour, and Amos Pell had come down from the chapel in what was obviously his best coat. Tobias stood among them, hugging the sandwich tin to his chest as if it contained the crown jewels and nothing less.

At five minutes to twelve, Mayor Alma Dunn appeared with a gold chain of office around her neck and Constable Brook walking at her side. The crowd parted to let them through like water around a ship, and somebody at the back began to clap. The sound spread, and for a moment the whole riverbank was applauding the idea of justice.

Then a car skidded to a halt at the end of the bridge, and Councillor Holt leapt out, followed by Dale Kane and a very pale Dr Ashe. He pushed through the crowd, red in the face, and shouted that the bridge was dangerous and that everyone must leave at once. His silver pen glittered in his fist like a small weapon, and for a moment Ines wondered whether he meant to throw it.

The mayor answered in a clear, calm voice that the bridge belonged to the town until Saturday, and that nobody had the right to clear it before then. She added that if Councillor Holt believed it to be dangerous, he was most welcome to wait upon the riverbank. A ripple of laughter ran through the crowd, and Holt's face took on the colour of a boiled beetroot.

Kane took a heavy step toward Ines, but Constable Brook raised one finger and said, with perfect politeness, that he would be wise to stay exactly where he was. He looked at the crowd, at the constable and at the ground between his enormous boots, and he stayed. It was the most obedient that anyone in Harrowby had ever seen him, and several people in the crowd tried hard not to smile.

Ines, Tobias, the mayor and the constable walked onto the bridge together while the entire town watched in silence from below. Ines lifted the hatch, and one by one they climbed down into the cold and rusty dark, where the river murmured on the other side of the stone. The sound of the crowd faded and was replaced by their own breathing and the slow, steady murmur of the river below.

Brook held a powerful torch, and its beam fell on the twelve small plates standing in their neat row, as patient as soldiers. Ines knelt in front of the twelfth and carefully scraped away the last flakes of the old paint from the slot, using the groove that Kane's knife had so kindly begun. She worked slowly and without hurrying, because she knew that nobody gets the chance to do something like this twice in a lifetime.

Tobias opened the sandwich tin and took out the real key, which was slightly greasy from the cheese, and handed it over with both hands. Ines held it up in the torchlight for a moment, the tiny bridge gleaming on its head, and then pushed it gently into the slot. She glanced at the others one more time, and they nodded together, as solemn and as hopeful as people at a christening.

For a moment nobody breathed, and the only sound was the river sliding by beyond the stone. Then Ines turned the key, slowly and with both hands, and with a soft and solid click that she would remember for the rest of her life, the lock opened. It had waited a hundred and fifty years to be asked, and it answered at once, as if it had been listening all that time.

The plate swung open on hidden hinges with a low groan, as though it were stretching after a very long sleep. Behind it, in the thickness of the stonework, lay a dry hollow about the size of a bread box. The air that rushed out smelled of cold iron and old, patient time, and Ines found that she was smiling without knowing why.

Brook's torch shone inside and picked out a small green iron box, with a simple clasp and a bridge cut into its lid. It had waited there, dry and safe, for a hundred and fifty years, while generations of Harrowby children had walked across the arches above it. Nobody said anything, because there was nothing grand enough to say, and the silence was in its way the best of all possible speeches.

Tobias lifted the box out with both hands, as though it were a sleeping child, and his fingers shook so badly that Ines had to steady the other side. Together they carried it to the foot of the ladder and passed it up to the mayor, who received it as if it were made of glass. Nobody hurried, and nobody spoke, and the little iron box passed from hand to hand as gently as a newborn child.

Up on the deck, in the bright noon light, Ines raised the clasp and opened the lid. Inside lay a yellow letter in Josiah Calder's neat handwriting and a folded parchment sealed with a disc of red wax. The wax was cracked across the middle, but it had held, and the little seal inside it still showed a perfect, shining bridge.

The crowd had crept onto the bridge, and a deep silence fell as the box was carried forward through the people. Holt stood at the very back with his arms folded and his face as hard as iron, while Kane shifted from one enormous boot to the other. Dr Ashe had turned her face toward the river, as though she hoped that the water would carry her away unseen.

The mayor took the letter, unfolded it with great care and cleared her throat twice before she could begin. Then she read aloud, in a voice that carried to the edge of the crowd and across the water, the words of a man who had died a century and a half ago. A child at the front whispered a question to its mother, and was gently hushed by half a dozen people at once.

In the letter Josiah Calder said that anyone who read these words had counted by the year and honoured a name, and that such a person was clever enough and patient enough to be trusted with his gift. He wrote with warmth and a dry humour, as though he were sitting with them on the parapet with his feet dangling over the river. The crowd leaned closer, hanging on every word, and even the pigeons on the railings seemed to have stopped their cooing.

He then gave the riverside meadows and the bridge to the people of Harrowby for ever, to be held on their behalf by the town and never to be sold. He asked only that the bridge be kept open, so that every child in the town might cross it on the way to school. The mayor paused here to steady her voice, and then she went on, a little more quietly than before.

Last of all, he wrote that his daughter Ada had walked every plank of the bridge while it was being built, and that it was really her bridge, and now theirs. Several people in the crowd wiped their eyes, and Tobias blew his nose with a noise like a trumpet. Even Walt Fenner, standing at the rail with his cap in his hands, was studying the water with great concentration.

The mayor held the parchment up to the sun, and the cracked red seal glowed like a small ember. It was a deed, she announced, and it declared that the meadows were held in trust for the people of Harrowby for ever, so that nobody could sell them. The crowd began to cheer, and Holt stood very still, with a face as white as paper.

Holt recovered quickly, as such men do, and shouted that the letter was a forgery, since anyone could write an old-fashioned letter and bury it under a bridge. His voice was loud, but his hand shook as he pointed at the box, and the silver pen slipped from his fingers and rolled across the planks. Nobody bent to pick it up, and it lay there glinting in the sun like something that had lost its power.

The mayor replied calmly that an expert from the county record office would examine both the letter and the deed before the day was out. Until then, she added, nobody was leaving, since Constable Brook was standing at the end of the bridge in a manner that discouraged argument. The constable gave a very small nod, and she folded her arms in the manner of a woman who intends to wait.

Then Dr Ashe stepped forward, her bracelets silent for once, and spoke to Tobias in a voice that trembled like a leaf. She said that she could not allow this to continue, and that after everything it was time somebody told the truth. Tobias looked at her as though he were seeing her for the first time.

She explained that she owed Councillor Holt a great deal of money, borrowed years ago to save the museum's roof, and that it had grown into a debt she could never repay. He had promised to forget it if she told him everything, and she had been too ashamed and too frightened to refuse. It was a very ordinary sort of wickedness, thought Ines, the kind that grows from fear and shame rather than from malice.

She had told him about the plates, the mill and the keyword Ada, and she had even told him where Ines was staying. She said it all quickly, as though the words were burning her mouth, and she did not look at Tobias once. When she finished, the bridge was so quiet that one could hear the river.

Ines told the crowd that she had begun to suspect Dr Ashe when she knew about the hotel break-in and the keyword before anybody had told her. The invented story about the coal store had finished the case, because only Dr Ashe had heard it, and that very night the museum cellar was broken open. A thief, she remarked, should always check that his source is not being tested.

Holt gave a snort and declared that this proved nothing, because it was merely the word of a frightened woman who wished to save her own skin. Kane, however, shifted his great weight from one foot to the other, and the old planks of the bridge gave a small and thoughtful creak. Every eye in the crowd went to his boots, and the silence on the bridge seemed to stretch like a drum skin.

Constable Brook took a photograph from her pocket, the one she had taken that morning of the boot print in the coal dust, and studied it with great care. Then she looked slowly up, and her gaze came to rest on the enormous boots of Dale Kane. The crowd, which had been following her eyes the way people follow a ball at a tennis match, gave a soft collective gasp.

She asked him politely to lift one foot, and he did so, because the whole town was watching and he could think of nothing else to do. The pattern on the sole matched the print exactly, down to a small, ragged tear in the rubber beneath the heel. Someone at the back whistled, long and low, and somebody else began to laugh before a neighbour hushed them both.

Brook told Kane in a level voice that he was under arrest for breaking into the hotel room and the museum cellar. His face turned the colour of a brick, and he shouted, to nobody's surprise, that he had only been following Councillor Holt's orders. Holt closed his eyes, as a man does when the sky he has been watching finally falls, and said nothing more.

Holt tried to slip away through the crowd, but the mayor called out in a ringing voice that he must stay where he was. He said that he would be speaking to his lawyers about every person on the bridge, and nobody paid the slightest attention. A small boy at the front stuck out his tongue and was not rebuked.

In the middle of the afternoon Ruth Hale arrived from the county record office, a small, spry woman with a leather case and a reputation for being impossible to hurry. She had spent thirty years looking at old paper, she said, and she had learned that it never lies, though it often exaggerates. Everyone made way for her at once, as a crowd will for a person who obviously knows exactly what she is about.

In the town hall she laid the parchment on a clean table under a bright lamp and studied it through a magnifying glass, saying nothing at all for twenty minutes. She examined the fibres of the paper, the colour of the ink and the way the letters leaned, and sometimes she hummed. Tobias hovered at her elbow like a nervous gull, and twice she gently pushed him away with a finger and a frown.

Then she compared the handwriting of the letter and the deed with the signed plans of the bridge and with Calder's little black notebook, laying them side by side. Ines counted the ticks of the town hall clock, which she suspected of being five minutes slow, and found that it made no difference. Time passed at its own pace in that room, and the afternoon light slid slowly across the floor like a patient cat.

At last Ruth turned her attention to the red wax seal, and she observed that it showed a tiny bridge in perfect miniature. Ines took the iron key from her pocket and held it beside the wax, and the little bridge on its head matched the seal in every line. A murmur of delight rippled around the room, and Tobias gripped the edge of the table so hard that his knuckles went white.

Ruth took off her glasses and announced that the deed and the letter were genuine without the slightest doubt. The paper, the ink and the signatures all belonged to the 1860s, she said, and two respectable witnesses, the town clerk and the minister of Saint Aldric's, had signed the deed in their own hands. It was as sound as the bridge itself, and one or two people in the room were seen to wipe their eyes.

The mayor read the legal words aloud, slowly, so that everyone in the room could follow every clause. The riverside meadows belonged to the people of Harrowby for ever, held in trust by the town, and no council could sell them, mortgage them or give them away. She read the last three words twice, because she enjoyed them so much, and the whole room joined in the second time.

At that moment Holt's telephone rang in his pocket, and he answered it with a trembling hand. It was the builder from the city, who said coldly that he had no interest in buying land that was tied up in a trust and that Holt should not telephone him again. The line went dead, and so, one felt, did something deep inside Holt, which until then had been very alive indeed.

That evening the council met in the town hall, and the room was so crowded that people stood on the stairs and leaned in at the windows. Mayor Dunn explained everything that had happened since the morning, in plain words and without ornament, and asked Holt whether he had anything to say. The silence that followed lasted a very long time, and in it one could hear the old clock on the wall tick.

Holt rose slowly, said in a thin voice that he was resigning from the council, and walked out into the evening without looking at anyone. Behind him the town hall clock struck eight, five minutes late, as it always did, and a few people laughed softly, with relief. Nobody followed him, and the door swung slowly shut behind him with a small click that sounded like the end of a chapter.

Late that night, Constable Brook knocked at the museum door with a large paper bag in her hand. Inside, wrapped in a sweater that smelled faintly of engine oil, was Ines's stolen laptop, which had been found in the back of Dale Kane's van. It was a little scratched, but it started at once, which Ines took as a sign that the day was ending well.

Ines carried it up to the workroom, made a mug of strong tea and sat down at the oak table under the lamp. Tobias left the lamp burning beside her and tiptoed away like a man leaving a sleeping baby. The museum creaked and ticked around her, as old buildings do at night, and she felt that the whole house was reading over her shoulder.

She typed the title of her report and began with the iron, which she described in loving detail. The rivets were tight, the ribs were free of cracks, and the old paint had protected the metal far better than anyone had a right to expect. It was the easiest paragraph she had ever written, because for once the facts and her duty pointed in exactly the same direction.

Next she described her inspection of the stone piers in the river, using plain words and exact measurements. The foundations were firm, the mortar was sound, and the current had done no real harm in a hundred and fifty years of trying. She added a note thanking Walt Fenner for his knowledge of the water, which no instrument could have equalled.

She recommended a fresh coat of paint, a handful of new bolts and a thorough cleaning of the drains, and nothing else whatever. Then she crossed out a sentence that sounded too eager and wrote a plainer one in its place, because honesty in an engineer should be as unadorned as a good beam. At two in the morning she was still polishing commas, and she knew that she would not sleep until the report was perfect.

At the very end she wrote the conclusion that she had known since the first morning, when she had tapped the first rivet and heard it ring. The bridge was safe, she stated, and with ordinary care it should stand for another hundred years. She signed her name, and she did not underline anything, because the truth of the report needed no help from her pen.

At nine o'clock the next morning Ines handed the report to Mayor Dunn in her office above the market square. The mayor read it twice, shook Ines's hand with both of hers and said that it was the best news she had received all week. Then she asked, with a twinkle in her eye, whether Ines had enjoyed her stay in Harrowby so far.

At a short meeting at noon, the council voted to keep the bridge open to everyone for as long as it stood. Several members who had sided with Holt only days before now declared loudly that they had never really wished to see it closed. The mayor accepted this with a gravity that was a little too complete, and her mouth twitched at one corner.

In a quiet corner of the police station, Dr Ashe gave Constable Brook a full and honest statement, and she did not leave out a single conversation. She resigned from the museum with a trembling hand, and the mayor said that she hoped the court would remember how much Dr Ashe had helped at the end. Tobias, who was watching through the half-open door, nodded slowly, and Ines saw in his eyes that he had already forgiven Dr Ashe.

Back at the museum, Tobias, who had been named acting director by a unanimous vote of the board, announced that the chamber with the twelve plates would be opened to visitors. The iron box, the little key and Calder's black notebook would go on show in the museum, beneath a sign that read Calder's Gift. He read the sign aloud three times, and each time it sounded like the first.

On Saturday afternoon the whole town carried tables and chairs onto the riverside meadows, in the manner of an army preparing a very cheerful siege. Bea Hollis hung flags between the trees as if she had been born to do it, and Walt Fenner tied a row of lanterns along the side of his boat. By three o'clock the grass was a patchwork of tablecloths, and the smell of sandwiches and cut grass hung warm in the air.

A brass band marched up the road, led by a small boy beating a very large drum with a look of deep concentration. A great crowd waited at the end of the bridge, and the children could hardly stand still, because the best part of any story is the part that is happening now. Ines stood among them, feeling oddly shy, as though she had wandered into a party where everyone but her knew the words.

Mayor Dunn stretched a red ribbon across the deck and cut it with a pair of enormous scissors, while a photographer from the local paper lay on the planks to catch the angle. She declared in a ringing voice that the bridge was open to everyone, for ever, as its builder had intended. The crowd roared its approval, and a flock of startled pigeons burst out from under the arches.

High on the hill, Amos Pell rang the old bell of Saint Aldric's with all the strength of his arms, and its deep voice rolled out across the valley. Every person in Harrowby knew exactly what it was saying, and for once nobody needed to be told. The sound seemed to come from the same century as the bridge and to belong to this one.

People streamed across the green iron bridge, waving flags and singing songs of which nobody knew all the words. Children raced along the planks, shrieking with delight, and Mrs Pike danced in the road with the man from the hardware store, who had finally put his pencil away. Even the pigeons returned, with the air of guests who had been wrongly dismissed.

On the meadows, long tables were laid with sandwiches, jellies and a cake the size of a cartwheel, which Bea had somehow baked in a single morning. Constable Brook told Ines quietly that Holt and Kane would soon have to explain everything to a court, and that she expected it to be a long and instructive afternoon for both of them. Ruth Hale, standing beside her, ate a very small slice of cake and looked as content as a cat in a sunbeam.

Tobias stood on a chair and gave a short speech about Josiah Calder and his daughter Ada, stumbling a little over his words and pushing his glasses up his nose with every sentence. He finished by raising a cup to the engineer who had tapped every rivet and refused to lie, and the whole meadow cheered until the swans left the river. Ines felt her face burn with pleasure and embarrassment, and she was not at all sorry that she had come to Harrowby.

Later, as the shadows grew long, Ines felt her phone buzz and read a message from an engineering firm in another town, whose name she knew and respected. They were offering her a new post, to begin at the end of the month, and asked for her answer by Monday. She put the phone away without replying and walked toward the water, where the evening light was turning the river to copper.

As the sun went down, Ines walked out onto the bridge alone, and after a minute or two Tobias came and stood beside her at the railing. The river beneath them had turned to gold and rose, and the arches threw long green shadows across the meadows. She told him, as gently as she could, that she had decided to take the job.

Tobias was quiet for a long moment, and then, in a voice that was almost steady, he asked her to come back. Ines looked at the lights of Harrowby coming on one by one beneath the darkening sky, at the old iron beneath her hands and at the man beside her. She promised that she would, and she meant it, and far above them the bell began to ring.
